extraction.name: HELVIPAD
extraction.description: A real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation, featuring 40K video frames from diverse environments including crowded indoor and outdoor scenes with various lighting conditions. Collected using two 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and a LiDAR sensor.
extraction.creator: Mehdi Zayene, Jannik Endres, Albias Havolli, Charles Corbière, Salim Cherkaoui, Alexandre Kontouli, Alexandre Alahi
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data were collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two omnidirectional cameras in a vertical arrangement, paired with a synchronized LiDAR sensor. The rig features two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup with a 19.1 cm baseline, capturing equirectangular images at 30 fps, paired with an Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor with a vertical field of view of 42.4°, operating at 10 fps, and mounted 45.0 cm below the bottom camera. A central processor manages data capture and ensures device synchronization. In total, 29 video sequences were collected.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Data collected across distinct scenes, encompassing indoor (e.g., corridors, halls) and outdoor (e.g., squares, external parking, footpaths) settings in various lighting conditions on a university campus. The dataset includes recordings taken at various times of the day, from early morning to night, under a variety of weather conditions, including cloudy and sunny skies.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Top images, bottom images, depth maps, and disparity maps are cropped to remove unnecessary borders and downsized from a width of 1024 pixels to 512 to enable more efficient training. The main challenge in processing raw data is to ensure a robust and accurate projection of the LiDAR point clouds on the 360° camera images. Initial rotation and translation transformations are applied to make the camera lens the coordinate system's center. The transformed points are then converted into spherical coordinates to match the structure of equirectangular images, and projected onto the equirectangular plane. The core step of the mapping process is the optimization of the rotation and translation parameters, achieved by minimizing the error between the projected points and their corresponding location on the equirectangular images.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Depth labels are obtained by projecting LiDAR point clouds onto equirectangular images. Disparity values are obtained from depth values via a specific equation relating spherical disparity to angular difference between 360° cameras point rays. A fully automated depth completion pipeline is applied to increase label density by interpolating depth on spherical grid points using temporally aggregated point clouds and applying a filtering process to exclude points with high uncertainty or lacking nearby measurements.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For depth completion, temporal aggregation fuses the current frame's point cloud with those from the four preceding and four succeeding frames. Interpolation estimates depth through a weighted average of k-nearest neighbors. Filtering ensures high-quality depth labels by excluding query points exceeding either an uncertainty criterion or an out-of-distribution threshold before mapping the remaining points to the image. Uncertainty estimation uses the relative weighted variance of interpolated depth values.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor, depth completion pipeline with temporal aggregation and interpolation
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Given the sparse nature of LiDAR point clouds compared to high-resolution camera images, ground-truth depth labels cover only a fraction of the total pixels. The depth completion approach is limited for fast-moving objects like cars. Occlusions were not explicitly handled, as the small LiDAR-camera baseline minimizes their impact. The dataset was collected on a university campus, which may limit generalization to other environments.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation. The dataset serves as a foundational resource for developing and benchmarking omnidirectional depth estimation models capable of navigating in human environments. Applications include autonomous driving, robotic navigation and exploration in complex indoor environments.
